The Architecture of Bee Space

To maintain a highly functional hive, we must adhere strictly to the rule of bee space ($\frac{3}{8}\text{ inch}$).

  • If the gap is too small ($<\frac{1}{4}\text{ inch}$), the bees will glue it shut with propolis.
  • If the gap is too large ($>\frac{1}{2}\text{ inch}$), they will fill it with structural burr/brace comb, making the frames impossible to remove cleanly.

1. Gaps Between Top Bars vs. Fully Enclosed?

The top of the frames must have gaps. They should never be fully enclosed.

Standard Langstroth frames rely on self-spacing side bars. The top portion of each side bar is manufactured to a width of $1\ \frac{3}{8}\text{ inches}$, while the top bar itself is narrower (typically $1\ \frac{1}{16}\text{ inches}$).

When you push the frames tightly against each other inside the box:

  • The wide shoulders of the side bars touch, automatically setting the correct center-to-center comb distance.
  • This naturally creates a $\frac{5}{16}\text{ to }\frac{3}{8}\text{ inch}$ gap between the top bars.

This gap serves as a vital vertical highway. Without it, the bees cannot move upward from the deep box (brood chamber) into the medium box (honey super) or access the inner cover.

3. Critical Clearance Zones for Construction

When assembling the outer wooden perimeters, keep these two critical spacing rules in mind:

Horizontal End-Space

The standard Langstroth box has an internal length of $18\ \frac{3}{8}\text{ inches}$. Your top bar rests on the rabbet joints (the notches or shelves cut into the short walls of the box). Your frame's total body width (excluding the top bar ears) should be roughly $17\ \frac{5}{8}\text{ inches}$. This leaves a precise $\frac{3}{8}\text{ inch}$ gap between the frame side bars and the inner hive walls.

Vertical Tier-Space

The difference between a deep box ($9\ \frac{5}{8}"$) and a deep frame ($9\ \frac{1}{8}"$) leaves a total variance of $\frac{1}{2}\text{ inch}$.

  • In a standard Top Bee Space configuration, the frame rests in the rabbet joint so that the top bar sits exactly $\frac{1}{4}\text{ to }\frac{3}{8}\text{ inch}$ below the top rim of the box.
  • This ensures that when you stack a medium box directly on top of the deep box, the total space between the bottom of the upper frames and the top of the lower frames stays perfectly within the bee space threshold.

Which style of top-bar joint (from your "Combined Top" sketches) are you planning to cut? I can provide the exact step-downs for your dado or rabbet cuts based on the thickness of your stock.

turns.prompt_text: Where could I Source wood for the frames? What I want mini long strips or a thick board?
turns.response_html:
Thick Boards vs. Mini Long Strips?

When milling components as precise as beehive frames, you should always start with a thick, wide board (typically 1x8 or 1x10 nominal, or 4/4 rough-sawn lumber) rather than buying pre-cut thin strips or laths.

Here is why starting thick is a strict requirement for this project:

  1. Safety on the Table Saw: Ripping the profile details—such as the tapered $1\ \frac{3}{8}"$ down to $1\ \frac{1}{16}"$ shoulders on the side bars or cutting the top bar grooves—is incredibly dangerous on thin, floppy material. A wide board gives you a solid handle to feed material past the blade safely, utilizing push pads and featherboards. You cut the intricate joints and profiles into the edge or face of a large board first, and then rip off your final $\frac{3}{8}"$ or $\frac{3}{4}"$ frame pieces as the very last step.
  2. Grain Direction and Warp Resistance: Pre-cut mini strips at big-box stores are often cut from fast-growth center trees, meaning they will twist, cup, and bow the moment they encounter hive humidity. Buying a wider board allows you to select straight, clear grain free of knots, ensuring your frame ends don't warp and throw off your $\frac{3}{8}\text{-inch}$ bee space.
  3. Yield Management: The standard depth frame top bar is $\frac{3}{4}\text{ inch}$ thick, but the side and bottom bars are a precise $\frac{3}{8}\text{ inch}$. A standard $1\text{-inch}$ nominal board (which is actually $\frac{3}{4}\text{ inch}$ thick) is perfect for this: you can use its full thickness for your top bars, and cleanly slice it down the middle to yield your $\frac{3}{8}\text{-inch}$ side and bottom bars.

Best Wood Species for Frames

  • Commercial Standard (Western Red Cedar or White Pine): Lightweight, decay-resistant, and incredibly stable. Pine is the most common commercial choice because it doesn't split easily when nailed or stapled.
  • Local Alternative (Basswood): If you can find it locally, basswood is prized by woodworkers for frames because it is extremely clean, lightweight, holds staples beautifully, and has absolutely no odor that might irritate a sensitive nucleus colony.

Sourcing Your Wood Locally

For the best results, skip the standard construction-grade 2x4 framing studs (which have too much moisture and sap) and look for Appearance Boards, Select Pine, or S4S (Surfaced 4 Sides) Hardwood/Softwood boards.

  • Munn Lumber Co. (Airport Road, Ames): A great first stop. Local lumberyards like this carry higher-tier, cleaner dimensional lumber and specialty softwoods/hardwoods that have been properly kiln-dried, which minimizes warping.
  • Liberty Hardwoods (Ankeny, IA): If you want to make an intentional drive out of town for premium material, this distributor handles exceptional quality hardwood and specialty project lumber. They are a staple for fine woodworking projects in central Iowa.
  • Lowe’s (Airport Road, Ames): If you go the big-box route, head straight to the indoor "Select Pine" or "Poplar" vertical racks. Inspect every board carefully down the edge like an arrow to ensure there is zero twist or bowing before buying.
